title: Beyond the 'To-Do List' Curriculum: Why School Mathematics Needs to Focus on Big Mathematical Ideas June 22, 2026, 6.26.26
author: Colin Foster
source: Centre for Mathematical Cognition Blog, Loughborough University (blog.lboro.ac.uk/cmc),
summary: Foster, a Professor of Mathematics Education at Loughborough University, argues that the school mathematics curriculum is typically experienced by students as a fragmented 'to-do list' of disconnected procedures -- pie charts on Monday, fractions on Tuesday, perpendicular bisectors on Wednesday -- with no visible thread connecting them, and that this fragmentation is as much a problem for teachers' mental models as for students' understanding. His proposed remedy, developed at his new site bigmathematicalideas.org, is to reorganize the entire curriculum around five 'Big Ideas': deep, cross-cutting concepts (like 'Thinking Multiplicatively') that recur across dozens of nominally unrelated topics, rather than around topic labels like 'fractions' or 'ratio.' He illustrates with the Thinking Multiplicatively idea, showing how weakness in relating numbers by multiplication (rather than addition) quietly underlies struggles across fractions, ratio, trigonometry, and percentage change -- meaning students often have the same handful of real gaps showing up under many different topic names. His practical claim is that investing substantial early time in securing the five Big Ideas pays off by making all the smaller, more granular topics that build on them faster and less painful to teach later, and that his site organizes the entire secondary curriculum's content by these five underlying ideas rather than by conventional topic headings, deliberately grouping topics that don't normally appear to be related.
points: Foster's central diagnosis is that curriculum fragmentation is not just a student comprehension problem but a teacher problem: if a teacher's own mental model of the curriculum is fragmented topic-by-topic, their capacity to teach for deep understanding is limited even when they are technically 'covering the content.'

His 'Big Idea' concept is explicitly not a topic label -- it is a cross-cutting concept (he names five, starting with 'Thinking Multiplicatively') that many disparate topics rest on, meaning a single underlying weakness can manifest as struggle across seemingly unrelated content areas like fractions, ratio, trigonometry, and percentage change.

His practical claim is a sequencing and time-investment argument: spending substantial early time securing the five Big Ideas is meant to make everything built on top of them faster, more efficient, and more satisfying to teach and learn later, rather than treating each topic as a separate object requiring separate remediation.

The bigmathematicalideas.org site deliberately reorganizes the entire secondary content list around the five Big Ideas rather than conventional topic headings, intentionally grouping topics teachers wouldn't normally think of as related.
quotes: To a student, these can feel like separate rooms in a sprawling house, with the doors locked between them. The curriculum becomes a fragmented ‘to-do list’ of disconnected procedures to be rehearsed for the next test and then promptly discarded.

This fragmentation isn’t just a student problem; it is a pedagogical one. If the teacher’s own mental model of the curriculum is fragmented, their ability to teach for deep understanding will be limited.
A Big Idea is not a topic title, like 'fractions'. It is an idea central to mathematics -- one that links across numerous different content areas.

Difficulties students have across diverse areas, such as fractions, ratio, trigonometry and percentage change, for instance, often relate more to trouble with thinking multiplicatively than to anything specific to those content areas.
Investing lots of time on the five Big Ideas aims to put students in the strongest possible position to learn all the smaller ideas much more efficiently and with greater satisfaction and success.
Let’s stop teaching the ‘to-do list’ and start teaching the Big Ideas!
